Without a return type, TypeScript works out what a function returns from its body. Change the body and the type changes with it, and the error shows up in the callers, far from the edit. With a return type, the error is on the `return` that no longer fits.

A function that already gets its type from somewhere else isn't reported, like a callback passed as an argument, or the value of a variable or property that has a type.

{/* Generated by src/codegen/lint-rule-docs.ts. Do not edit this section. */}

## Configure

Off by default. To turn it on:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/explicit-function-return-type" = "error" # or "warn"
```

Every option, set to its default:

```toml bunfig.toml
[lint.rules]
"@typescript-eslint/explicit-function-return-type" = ["error", {
  allowExpressions = false,
  allowTypedFunctionExpressions = true,
  allowHigherOrderFunctions = true,
  allowDirectConstAssertionInArrowFunctions = true,
  allowConciseArrowFunctionExpressionsStartingWithVoid = false,
  allowFunctionsWithoutTypeParameters = false,
  allowIIFEs = false,
  allowedNames = [], # list of strings
}]
```

{/* End of the generated section. */}

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad {"count": 3} */}
```ts
function total(prices: number[]) {
  return prices.reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0);
}

const isEmpty = (items: string[]) => items.length === 0;

class Cart {
  size() {
    return 0;
  }
}
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```ts
function total(prices: number[]): number {
  return prices.reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0);
}

const isEmpty = (items: string[]): boolean => items.length === 0;

type Check = (items: string[]) => boolean;
const isFull: Check = items => items.length > 9;

class Cart {
  size(): number {
    return 0;
  }
}
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `allowExpressions` | `false` | Allow a function expression, unless it's the value of a variable, a class member or an `export default`. |
| `allowTypedFunctionExpressions` | `true` | Allow a function expression that gets its type from a typed variable or property, from an `as`, or from the call it's passed to. |
| `allowHigherOrderFunctions` | `true` | Allow a function that returns another function right away. The inner function is still checked. |
| `allowDirectConstAssertionInArrowFunctions` | `true` | Allow `() => value as const`. |
| `allowConciseArrowFunctionExpressionsStartingWithVoid` | `false` | Allow `() => void save()`. |
| `allowFunctionsWithoutTypeParameters` | `false` | Only check generic functions. |
| `allowIIFEs` | `false` | Allow a function that's called where it's written: `(() => { ... })()`. |
| `allowedNames` | `[]` | Names of functions and methods that are never reported. |

With `allowHigherOrderFunctions`, only the function that does the work needs a type:

{/* good */}
```ts
const multiplyBy = (factor: number) => (value: number): number => value * factor;
```

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowHigherOrderFunctions": false}]} */}
```ts
const multiplyBy = (factor: number) => (value: number): number => value * factor;
```

With `allowExpressions`, a function inside a larger expression is allowed. One that's stored under a name is still reported:

{/* good {"options": [{"allowExpressions": true}]} */}
```ts
const steps = [() => "load", () => "render"];
```

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowExpressions": true}]} */}
```ts
const load = () => "load";
```

With `allowFunctionsWithoutTypeParameters`:

{/* good {"options": [{"allowFunctionsWithoutTypeParameters": true}]} */}
```ts
const label = (id: number) => `#${id}`;
```

{/* bad {"options": [{"allowFunctionsWithoutTypeParameters": true}]} */}
```ts
const first = <T,>(items: T[]) => items[0];
```

## When not to use it

Writing out every return type is a lot of typing in code that only one file uses. To check only what a module exports, use `@typescript-eslint/explicit-module-boundary-types` instead.
